title: When the US Mail Was Delivered Underground at 35 MPH Through a Network of Pneumatic Tubes (1893–1953)
description:
in History, Technology |   	August 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Twen­ty years ago, Unit­ed States sen­a­tor Ted Stevens drew long-last­ing
body:
in History, Technology |   	August 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Twen­ty years ago, Unit­ed States sen­a­tor Ted Stevens drew long-last­ing online ridicule by describ­ing the inter­net as “a series of tubes.” While some com­men­ta­tors not­ed that the anal­o­gy was­n’t quite as out­landish as it seemed, most react­ed with noth­ing more than amused baf­fle­ment. Where had Stevens come up with that image? Giv­en that he was born in 1923, per­haps he was draw­ing on mem­o­ries of a tech­no­log­i­cal won­der of his child­hood: the under­ground pneu­mat­ic sys­tems through which mail was deliv­ered in major Amer­i­can cities from the eigh­teen-nineties until the ear­ly nine­teen-fifties, whose sto­ry is told in the It’s His­to­ry video above.
Such series of tubes entered ser­vice in Lon­don, Paris, and Berlin in the mid-nine­teenth cen­tu­ry. In 1893, Philadel­phia became the first Amer­i­can city to get one, thanks to the advo­ca­cy of tech­no­log­i­cal­ly mind­ed depart­ment store mag­nate-turned-Post­mas­ter Gen­er­al John Wana­mak­er. At the inau­gu­ra­tion, writes Hid­den City’s Har­ry Kyr­i­akodis, Wana­mak­er “placed a Bible wrapped in an Amer­i­can flag into a can­is­ter that went fly­ing (under­ground) to the Cen­tral Post Office with a loud ‘whish’.” Philadel­phi­a’s net­work expand­ed apace, even­tu­al­ly includ­ing near­ly twen­ty miles of tun­nels, and “New York City, Boston, Chica­go, and St. Louis adopt­ed sim­i­lar deliv­ery sys­tems by 1898, all oper­at­ed by the Post Office Depart­ment.”
Oper­at­ed at a seri­ous loss, that is: when the U.S. got involved in World War I, the Post Office sus­pend­ed pneu­mat­ic ser­vice to con­serve resources. Only in the twen­ties did the tubes start whish­ing again in parts of New York and Boston, whose high vol­umes of mail could poten­tial­ly jus­ti­fy the oper­a­tion. In fact, the sheer amount of mail even­tu­al­ly got to be too much for the steel cap­sules and the cast-iron tun­nels through which com­pressed air pushed them. As retired U.S. Postal Inspec­tor Robert A. Cohen explains it in his his­to­ry of these sys­tems, “It takes a cer­tain amount of time for a gal­lon of liq­uid to trav­el through a fun­nel. Two gal­lons take twice as long to pass through. The val­ue of the Pneu­mat­ic Tube Ser­vice decreased as mail vol­ume increased.”


	

The pro­lif­er­a­tion of auto­mo­biles and the expan­sion of their sup­port­ing infra­struc­ture dealt an even more seri­ous blow: after World War II, deliv­er­ing mail on the roads had clear­ly become more effi­cient than doing it under­ground. Some “rock­e­teers,” as the sys­tem’s oper­a­tors were called, stuck it out until Decem­ber 12, 1953, when pneu­mat­ic mail ser­vice was offi­cial­ly sus­pend­ed all across the coun­try.

This marked the end of an era, espe­cial­ly for the rock­e­teers said to have used the net­work to sur­rep­ti­tious­ly receive orders from their favorite sand­wich shops. Remem­ber­ing Ted Stevens’ noto­ri­ous remark, it’s tempt­ing to describe the series of tubes that were pneu­mat­ic mail deliv­ery sys­tems as an ear­ly ver­sion of the inter­net — and even more so it was already get­ting peo­ple hooked on food deliv­ery.
]

title: The Most Controversial Ancient Philosophy: Epicureanism
description:
in History, Philosophy |   	August 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Over the years, you’ve prob­a­bly heard at least a few peo­ple casu­al­ly d
body:
in History, Philosophy |   	August 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Over the years, you’ve prob­a­bly heard at least a few peo­ple casu­al­ly describe them­selves as Epi­cure­ans. As used today, the label can refer to as lit­tle as enjoy­ing the occa­sion­al expen­sive restau­rant meal. The bar was a bit high­er in the sec­ond cen­tu­ry, as explained by ancient-his­to­ry YouTu­ber Gar­rett Ryan in the new video above from his chan­nel Told in Stone. But there is, at least, one major aspect of the orig­i­nal doc­trine laid out by Epi­cu­rus (341–270 BC) with which most any of his self-styled fol­low­ers in our time would agree: that plea­sure is the great­est good. Whether they would fol­low that premise all the way to the con­clu­sions Epi­cu­rus did is anoth­er mat­ter.
For that ancient Greek philoso­pher, Ryan explains, “hap­pi­ness was the sole legit­i­mate goal of human exis­tence. The essence of hap­pi­ness is free­dom from anx­i­ety. Since the great­est source of men­tal dis­tur­bance is fear about death and the after­life, it is nec­es­sary to under­stand the true nature of the uni­verse.”
There­after come the prin­ci­ples about atoms drift­ing through the infi­nite void, a sub­ject of less inter­est to many twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry “Epi­cure­ans” than the mechan­ics of the Williams-Sono­ma rewards pro­gram. Still, they would do well to learn at least one rel­e­vant Greek term: atarax­ia, or the “tran­quil­i­ty that comes from being suf­fi­cient in one­self.”
Achiev­ing atarax­ia is not a mat­ter of mere­ly indulging the sens­es. Rather, “all sources of unnec­es­sary men­tal dis­tur­bance should be removed.” That means no pol­i­tics and prob­a­bly no mar­riage, though friend­ship is accept­able. Though fair­ly ascetic in its orig­i­nal form, Epi­cure­anism drew quite a few high-pro­file Romans as adher­ents — and as detrac­tors. No less a fig­ure than Cicero, for exam­ple, attacked both its oppo­si­tion to tra­di­tion­al Roman reli­gion and, per­haps pre­dictably, its iso­la­tion from pub­lic life. Plutarch went so far as to write anti-Epi­cure­an trea­tis­es, includ­ing one titled “It Is Not Pos­si­ble to Live Plea­sur­ably Accord­ing to the Doc­trines of Epi­cu­rus.” That may or may not be true by our mod­ern stan­dards, but the ques­tion is worth con­tem­plat­ing over a good din­ner.

title: Watch Stewart Brand’s 6‑Part Series How Buildings Learn, With Music by Brian Eno
description:
in Architecture, Film |   	August 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Stew­art Brand came onto the cul­tur­al scene dur­ing the 1960s, help­ing to
body:
in Architecture, Film |   	August 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Stew­art Brand came onto the cul­tur­al scene dur­ing the 1960s, help­ing to stage the Acid Tests made famous by Ken Kesey and the Mer­ry Pranksters, and lat­er launch­ing the influ­en­tial Whole Earth Cat­a­log (some­thing Steve Jobs described as “Google in paper­back form, 35 years before Google came along”). He also vig­or­ous­ly cam­paigned in 1966 to have NASA release a pho­to­graph show­ing the entire­ty of Earth from space—some­thing we take for grant­ed now, but fired human­i­ty’s imag­i­na­tion back then.


	

Dur­ing the 1970s and beyond, Brand found­ed CoEvo­lu­tion Quar­ter­ly, a suc­ces­sor to the Whole Earth Cat­a­log; the WELL (“Whole Earth ‘Lec­tron­ic Link”), “a pro­to­typ­i­cal, wide-rang­ing online com­mu­ni­ty for intel­li­gent, informed par­tic­i­pants the world over;” and even­tu­al­ly The Long Now Foun­da­tion, whose work we’ve high­light­ed here before. When not cre­at­ing new insti­tu­tions, he has poured his cre­ative ener­gies into books and films.
Above you can watch How Build­ings Learn, Brand’s six-part BBC TV series from 1997, which comes com­plete with music by Bri­an Eno. Based on his illus­trat­ed book shar­ing the same title, the TV series offers a cri­tique of mod­ernist approach­es to archi­tec­ture (think Buck­min­ster Fuller, Frank Gehry, and Le Cor­busier) and instead argues for “an organ­ic kind of build­ing, based on four walls, which is easy to change and expand and grow as the ide­al form of build­ing.”


	

Brand made the series avail­able on his YouTube chan­nel, with these words: “Any­body is wel­come to use any­thing from this series in any way they like… Hack away. Do cred­it the BBC, who put con­sid­er­able time and tal­ent into the project.” And he added the note­wor­thy foot­note: “this was one of the first tele­vi­sion pro­duc­tions made entire­ly in digital—shot dig­i­tal, edit­ed dig­i­tal.”
Find the first three parts above, and the remain­ing parts below:

Part 1: Flow
Part 2: The Low Road
Part 3: Built for Change
Part 4: Unre­al Estate
Part 5: The Romance of Main­te­nance

title: One of the Best Preserved Ancient Manuscripts of The Iliad Is Now Digitized: See the “Bankes Homer” Manuscript in High Resolution (Circa 150 C.E.)
description: Each time I sit through the end cred­its of a film, I think about how weird auteur the­o­ry is—that a work of cin­e­ma can be pri­mar­i­ly though
body:
Each time I sit through the end cred­its of a film, I think about how weird auteur the­o­ry is—that a work of cin­e­ma can be pri­mar­i­ly thought of as the sin­gu­lar vision of the direc­tor. Typ­i­cal exam­ples come from arti­er fare than the usu­al Hol­ly­wood block­buster in which crews of thou­sands of stunt­peo­ple, spe­cial effects tech­ni­cians, and ani­ma­tors (and sev­er­al dozen “pro­duc­ers”) make essen­tial con­tri­bu­tions. In the case of, say, Wes Ander­son or David Lynch—or ear­li­er direc­tors like Godard or Kubrick—one can’t deny the evi­dence of a sin­gu­lar mind at work. Even so, we tend to ele­vate direc­tors to the sta­tus of god­like arti­fi­cers, sur­round­ed by a few angel­ic helpers behind the cam­era and a few star actors in front of it. Every­one else is an extra, includ­ing, very often, the actu­al writ­ers of a film.
Of course, the notion of the auteur comes from the gen­er­al the­o­ry of author­ship that iden­ti­fies lit­er­ary works as the prod­uct of a sin­gle intel­lect. French the­o­rists like Michel Fou­cault and Roland Barthes have cast sus­pi­cion on this idea. When it comes to writ­ing from the man­u­script age, hun­dreds or thou­sands of years old, it can be next to impos­si­ble to iden­ti­fy the author of a work.
Many an ancient work comes down to us as the prod­uct of “Anony­mous.” In the case of the major Greek epics, The Odyssey and The Ili­ad, we have a name, Homer, that most clas­sics schol­ars treat as a con­ve­nient place­hold­er. As a Uni­ver­si­ty of Cincin­nati clas­sics site not­ed, “Homer” could stand for “a group of poets whose works on the theme of Troy were col­lect­ed.”
Though writ­ten ref­er­ences to Homer date back to the 6th cen­tu­ry B.C., giv­ing cre­dence to the his­tor­i­cal exis­tence of the leg­endary blind poet, he might have been more direc­tor than author, bring­ing togeth­er into a coher­ent whole the labor of hun­dreds of dif­fer­ent sto­ry­tellers. For his­to­ri­an Adam Nicol­son, author of Why Homer Mat­ters, “it’s a mis­take to think of Homer as a per­son. Homer is an ‘it.’ A tra­di­tion. An entire cul­ture com­ing up with ever more refined and ever more under­stand­ing ways of telling sto­ries that are impor­tant to it. Homer is essen­tial­ly shared.” The nar­ra­tive poet­ry attrib­uted to Homer, Nicol­son sug­gests, might go back a thou­sand years before the poet sup­pos­ed­ly put it to papyrus.
You can read this Nation­al Geo­graph­ic inter­view with Nicol­son (or buy his book) to fol­low the argu­ment. It isn’t par­tic­u­lar­ly original—as Daniel Mendel­sohn writes at The New York­er, “the dom­i­nant ortho­doxy” for over a hun­dred years “has been that The Ili­ad evolved over cen­turies before final­ly being writ­ten down” some­time around 700 B.C. We have no man­u­scripts from that ear­ly peri­od, and no one knows how much the poem evolved through scrib­al errors in the trans­mis­sion from man­u­script to man­u­script over cen­turies. This is one of many ques­tions lit­er­ary his­to­ri­ans ask when they approach papyri like that at the top—an excerpt from the so-called “Bankes Homer,” the best-pre­served spec­i­men of a por­tion of The Ili­ad, con­tain­ing Book 24, lines 127–804, and dat­ing from cir­ca 150 C.E.
Pur­chased in Egypt in 1821 by Egyp­tol­o­gist William John Bankes, and acquired by an adven­tur­er named Gio­van­ni Finati on the island of Ele­phan­tine, the papyrus scroll, which you can see in full and in high res­o­lu­tion at the British Library site, was cre­at­ed like most oth­er “lit­er­ary papyri” for hun­dreds of years. As the British Library describes the process:
Pro­fes­sion­al scribes made copies from exem­plars at the request of clients, tran­scrib­ing by hand, word by word, let­ter by let­ter. Until around the 2nd cen­tu­ry CE these man­u­script books took the form of rolls com­posed of papyrus sheets past­ed one to the oth­er in suc­ces­sion, often over a con­sid­er­able length.
In addi­tion to the text itself, notes the site His­to­ry of Infor­ma­tion, the man­u­script con­tains “breath­ing marks and accents made by an ancient diorthotes or ‘cor­rec­tor’ to show cor­rect poet­ic pro­nun­ci­a­tion.” The ancient prac­tice of “cor­rect­ing” was a ped­a­gog­i­cal tech­nique used for train­ing stu­dents to prop­er­ly read the text. Like­ly for hun­dreds of years before there was a text, the poem would be com­mit­ted to mem­o­ry, and recit­ed by anony­mous bards all over the Greek-speak­ing world, prob­a­bly chang­ing in the telling to suit the tastes and bias­es of dif­fer­ent audi­ences. Who can say how many, if any, of those ancient bards bore the name “Homer”?
Again you can see the Bankes Homer in high res­o­lu­tion here (click the image to view in a larg­er for­mat).

title: Stuffed Animals and Found Objects Reconfigure in Sungho Bae's Uncanny Sculptures
description: Like many kids, I struggled with bedtime. I was a naturally anxious child with a vast imagination and siblings who loved to watch scary movies, le
body:
Like many kids, I struggled with bedtime. I was a naturally anxious child with a vast imagination and siblings who loved to watch scary movies, leaving me capable of generating an endless array of terrifying things that could happen once the lights went out. To remedy this problem, my mother designated a particular stuffed bear as my guardian, and before retreating to her own room, she would grab its squishy body and infuse it with her protective “power” should I need some comfort and safety during the night. For a time at least, this plush toy was enough to get me to sleep.
For Seoul-born, Chicago-based artist Sungho Bae, the meaning and emotion we ascribe to our childhood possessions gets flipped inside out. Bae gathers once-beloved toys from shops and disposal sites, which he then deconstructs and reconfigures atop a figurative armature. What emerges are uncanny sculptures and reliefs made of a vibrant, fleshy patchwork that resembles organs, tissue, muscle, and more.
Detail of “Head of an Invoker”
In his exhibition Apotropaia, Bae presents a suite of new works likened to charms, amulets, and other magical forms that ward off evil. The title references the ancient Greek belief in mystical powers and nods to the ways in which humankind has long found meaning in objects, rituals, and materials. Why were these presumably cherished toys discarded? And how might their former significance be reshaped?
One of the less abstract and fantastical works is “Dansu,” a head and cross-cut neck with taxidermy eyes and feathers standing in for hair. The piece references a state in the Korean game of Go in which there’s only one move left before capture. Presented atop a weathered game board, the figure embodies the tension between natural and artificial and spirit and death, as he stares with vacant glass eyes originally designed to replicate life in a mounted animal.
Additional wall works, each titled “Gut,” are more amorphous. With wispy hair encircling an edge and bits of clay embedding into the mishmash of color and texture, the strange pieces revel in their ambiguity, inviting the viewer in for a closer look.
Apotropaia is on view through September 6 at 4th Ward Project Space. Keep up with Bae on Instagram.

title: Get Up Close to the Sun in the Highest Resolution Image Ever Captured
description: Scientists have long studied how magnetic energy powers solar activity. The constant motion of plasma particles and the sun’s rotation are major c
body:
Scientists have long studied how magnetic energy powers solar activity. The constant motion of plasma particles and the sun’s rotation are major contributors to its cycles and events, such as flares and coronal mass ejections, which lob huge quantities of plasma and gas into space.
Sometimes these explosions reach the earth’s magnetic field and cause geomagnetic storms, which are when we see some of the most brilliant auroras. But they also disrupt or damage our communications systems, power grids, GPS, and satellites, and researchers want to further understand how the sun builds up its magnetic energy so we better know how to guard against its massive fits of activity. They’ve also been trying to figure out why the sun’s corona, or atmosphere, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface.



Thanks to the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which has pride of place at the National Solar Observatory on Maui, Hawaii, the highest-resolution image of the sun ever captured has revealed unique features that may give solar scientists some insight into how this magnetic energy builds.
Rippling forms that physicists call Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability (KHI) demonstrate the effect of two fluids flowing past each other at different velocities. It’s a phenomenon named for the two scientists who observed it for the first time around 1870, and it can be seen in clouds, ocean waves, and the atmospheres of gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn. 
The Inouye telescope, the most powerful of its kind, was able to capture features smaller than 12 miles across, providing insights that remained hidden in earlier photos. The details may illuminate part of a solar process that scientists refer to as “flux braiding,” because the way the sun’s magnetic field lines move around one another result in a plaited effect. But the tension builds and builds before eventually breaking, which is when we see flares and similar events. The swirls of KHI may have something to do with how these twists happen in the first place.
“This could solve this biggest mystery of the last half a century for solar physics and astrophysics,” team scientist Dr. David Kuridze told The Guardian. “When you have this instability in the system, it is very easy to cascade the energy into smaller scales. And at some point, it just dissipates as a heat. This could make hot coronas, hot outer atmospheres of the sun and similar stars.”

title: Discover Millions of Artworks from Thousands of Museums with This Huge Art Search Engine
description: Described by its anonymous creators as “the largest search engine for museum art,” The Last Museum is a veritable trove of the the world’s great w
body:
Described by its anonymous creators as “the largest search engine for museum art,” The Last Museum is a veritable trove of the the world’s great works. It currently includes pieces by more than 290,000 artists, which are held across 4,903 museums and represent 304 cultures and nationalities. A lot of the works are in the public domain, such as a 19th-century beaded bag attributed to the Lakota, thousands of ancient Etruscan artifacts, and objects spanning thousands of years in places like Germany, Spain, India, and Egypt.
Clicking on any artifact will any available information about the artist, title, and date, plus a link to the museum collection it belongs to. If there’s copyright attached to the images, they’re available in accordance with fair use, which means they’re available at a low resolution for browsing online but not reproducing, and they’re shared strictly for educational and non-commercial purposes. “We currently have around five million artworks indexed, and strive to eventually index all museum art in the world,” the creators say.
